content: 1. Training programs addressing violence against women (VAW) should be led by a multidisciplinary team. This team must include experts in VAW, specialists in data collection and management (including IT professionals if electronic systems are used), representatives from civil society organizations (CSOs) or survivors to ensure their perspectives are represented, and professionals responsible for responding to, documenting, and managing VAW-related administrative data. 2. The training should emphasize the importance of VAW data collection in achieving national and sectoral priorities, as well as the priorities of service providers. This will help motivate personnel to collect and manage administrative data effectively. 3. Job aids, templates, and case studies should be provided to illustrate how data collection tools have been applied in practice. This includes ensuring privacy and confidentiality, such as not discussing violence in front of other staff or leaving records unsecured. 4. Service managers should create policies and environments that support survivor privacy and confidentiality, prevent stigma and discrimination, and address barriers to privacy in the local context. 5. Training should include opportunities for role-playing and practicing data collection and entry. Scripts should be provided to guide interactions with survivors, explaining how their information will be recorded, stored, and shared, with an emphasis on obtaining survivor consent and maintaining confidentiality. 6. Implementation plans for training must recognize that capacity building for improving VAW services and data collection cannot be achieved in a single session. Ongoing training and support are essential. 7. Building relationships between VAW experts and data specialists, such as national statistical offices (NSOs), can facilitate sustained capacity development and support for improving data collection and use. 8. A study conducted in India (2018-2019) demonstrated the effectiveness of training healthcare providers to identify and respond to domestic or intimate partner violence. Post-training, providers showed significant improvements in knowledge, attitudes, and skills, and were more likely to identify survivors and provide support services. 9. The study also highlighted the importance of documenting cases of violence in secure, standardized registers. Nurses were assigned responsibility for maintaining these registers under lock and key, and supervisors conducted quality checks to ensure accuracy and completeness. 10. Challenges in busy healthcare settings, such as hesitancy among nurses to document cases and the separation of social worker records from medical files, were resolved through discussions with hospital administrators. 11. Over nine months, 531 women were identified through documentation, with 74% reporting emotional/psychological violence, 64% reporting physical violence, and 12% reporting sexual violence. This underscores the importance of high-quality training and adapting workflows to specific contexts. 12. Digital record systems can address challenges observed in paper-based systems, such as illegible handwriting and missing data, by ensuring better standardization and accuracy. 13. Planning for VAW administrative data systems must include considerations for human, infrastructure, and financial resources. Initial investments in these areas are necessary to achieve long-term cost savings and improved data quality. 14. Regular reporting of VAW administrative data incentivizes data production and use, creating a virtuous cycle that supports improved policy and practice. 15. Coordination mechanisms for VAW administrative data should include CSOs with expertise in addressing VAW, especially in contexts where they provide a significant proportion of services. Efforts must be made to minimize the additional workload for CSOs and other service providers. 16. Monitoring, support, and ongoing training are required to ensure data quality and continuous improvement. This includes regular oversight, spot checks, and addressing systemic issues through training and system updates. 17. A case study from Moldova (2017-2018) demonstrated the value of methodological guidance and training in improving VAW data collection and quality. This included developing detailed written guidance, improving data sheets with error-checking formulas, and training employees responsible for data entry and management. 18. Effective VAW administrative data systems require collaboration among government officials, service providers, and community representatives to address challenges and improve data flow and completeness.
